text:
In economies where energy consumption, productive transformation, and
recorded GDP remain located within the same national boundary, the GDP-
energy relationship remains visible.
This appears in the current results for
China and India.
In mature service economies, the relation may weaken or become negative. This
does not necessarily mean that energy has become irrelevant. It may mean that
the place where energy is consumed, the place where productive transformation
occurs, and the place where monetary value is recorded have become territorially
separated.
This connects directly with Campergue’s Cash/Money distinction. GDP is ex-
pressed in monetary units and accounting conventions. It is a Cash-like repre-
sentation in national accounts. Money, in Campergue’s vocabulary, refers to
purchasing power or economic value. Productive transformation, however, may
occur elsewhere. A country can record monetary value domestically while the
energy-intensive Work supporting that value is performed abroad.
The global result is therefore essential. At the world level, production cannot be
shifted outside the accounting boundary. This is why the world-level coupling
is the strongest evidence in the current note.
A useful conceptual chain is:
Energy inputs and technical systems
-> Economic Work / productive transformation
-> changes in cost, utility, speed, output, and capacity
-> real production and value added
-> Money / purchasing power
-> Cash / monetary recording in accounts
In global value chains, this chain can be territorially split:
Energy and transformation in country A
-> product, component, logistics, infrastructure
-> design, brand, margin, finance, distribution in country B
-> GDP and monetary value recorded in country B
This is why a weak national energy-GDP correlation cannot be interpreted as
complete dematerialization. It may reflect a broken territorial alignment be-
tween Cash, Money, Economic Work, and energy.
7. Discussion
The empirical findings support three claims.
First, there is strong evidence of world-level GDP-energy coupling in the current
World Bank run. The log-log association is very high, and the annual log-change
model remains materially meaningful.

1. It may improve energy efficiency.
2. It may shift from industry to services.
3. It may outsource energy-intensive production.
4. It may import embodied energy in goods.
5. It may record high value added in activities whose material base is located else-
where.
6. It may benefit from global supply chains that conceal production energy outside
national accounts.
This distinction is directly relevant to Campergue’s corpus. If one focuses only on
accounting flows, the economy appears increasingly immaterial. If one focuses on
transformations, the material and energetic base remains visible, but often outside
the national boundary where value is booked.
The empirical results therefore support a careful formulation:
The materiality of growth has not disappeared.
It has become less visible in national accounts.
This does not mean that every unit of GDP requires the same amount of energy as in
the past. Energy efficiency, technological change, and structural transformation are
real. The result is subtler: global growth still appears difficult to describe without ref-
erence to energy use, even when some national economies show apparent territorial
decoupling.
7
Relation to Campergue’s corpus
The empirical analysis should be read as a limited test of a macroeconomic implica-
tion, not as a validation of the full theoretical system.
Campergue’s corpus argues that economic reasoning must distinguish monetary sup-
ports from real value, labour from economic Work, and accounting movement from
productive transformation. The GDP-energy results are compatible with that orien-
tation: they suggest that real economic growth remains connected to material and
energetic transformations.
However, the regressions do not prove:
• the full Work →Money formalism;
• the complete distinction between productive and non-productive agents;
• the proposed transformation equations;
• the validity of all definitions in the corpus;
• causality from energy to GDP;
• the absence of feedback from GDP to energy use.
The results provide empirical support for a narrower statement:
At the world scale, real GDP and energy use remain strongly coupled in the tested data.
This is enough to justify including the code as an empirical appendix to the corpus.

2.3 Transactions and transformations
Conventional accounts often describe economies as flows: goods flow, services
flow, money flows, income flows. Campergue’s corpus asks what transformations
generate those flows. A transaction can transfer ownership or settle a claim
without modifying the product. A transformation changes the product, process,
utility, cost, speed, or productive capacity.
This distinction is crucial for interpreting GDP. GDP records value added, but
it does not always make clear where the underlying energy-intensive transfor-
mations occurred. In a global value chain, design, brand, finance, distribution,
and margins can be recorded in one country while extraction, manufacturing,
logistics, and energy use occur elsewhere.
The question is not whether services are “fake” or useless.
The question is
whether national accounts can separate the place where Cash is recorded from
the place where Economic Work occurs.
3. Literature position
3.1 Energy and economic growth
The energy-growth literature is large and methodologically diverse. Stern’s mul-
tivariate approach to U.S. energy and GDP is one early reference point. Later
surveys by Payne and Ozturk emphasize that conclusions vary with country,
period, variables, and econometric specification. This matters for the present
paper: no single regression establishes a universal causal law.
Other work has identified stable broad relationships between income and energy
use. Csereklyei, Rubio-Varas, and Stern describe stylized facts linking energy
use and economic growth over long periods.
Decoupling literature adds nu-
ance: Haberl and co-authors’ systematic review finds that relative decoupling
is observed in some domains, but strong absolute decoupling is much harder to
establish, especially when useful energy and exergy are considered.
Recent public research commentary reaches a related conclusion at the global
level: apparent decoupling in rich economies can be weakened once offshoring
and embodied energy are considered. The UK Energy Research Centre also re-
ports that energy eﬀiciency can itself contribute to GDP growth, complicating
the simplistic idea that eﬀiciency necessarily breaks the energy-growth relation-
ship.
The implication is not that energy mechanically “causes” GDP. Rather, GDP
and energy are co-determined inside the same production system. The present
paper therefore estimates association and comovement, not one-way causality.
